Well, hello doctor. Thank you for seeing me. I, um... well, to be perfectly honest, what brought me in is that my head just feels terribly foggy lately. Just this thick, heavy fog. And I know people like to say, 'oh, you're 79, you're just getting older,' but it's not that. It's different. I keep mixing up the most simple things, things I've managed just fine for years. 

I do a lot of volunteer work down at the community center—mostly helping organize the local art displays and coordinating the front desk—and lately, I've been making a complete mess of it. I'll get the exhibit dates completely wrong, putting the spring showcase in the winter slot in my mind, or I'll be going down the phone list and I just... I completely lose track of which volunteer I already called. I ended up calling poor Linda twice in fifteen minutes last Tuesday. She was very sweet about it, but it's embarrassing! 

And it's my own schedule, too. My appointment times are all jumbled. I was so worried I'd mess up the time for this very appointment that I had to write it down on three different calendars and stick a note on my fridge. It’s just... it’s like trying to think through molasses, and it's really starting to upset my day-to-day life, because I'm usually very organized, you know? I ran my household like a clock for decades, but now everything just gets mixed up the second it enters my brain, and I just... I don't know why it's happening.

Well, yes, I suppose focus is exactly what it is. Or rather, the lack of it! Like I was saying before about the fog... it’s just so hard to keep my mind on a straight track. I end up staring at the paper, feeling completely lost in my own head. So yes, focusing is terribly difficult right now. No, no, I wouldn't say that at all. The words are right there. In fact, my daughter always says I have the gift of gab, and I suppose she's right! I've never been one to be at a loss for words. Distracted by my surroundings? Oh, heavens no. It really isn't the environment that's the problem. It's not the outside world pulling me away, if that makes sense. 

Like I mentioned, I do all my planning and organizing at that little oak table by the window. Now, I suppose you would think sitting by a front window would be terribly distracting, wouldn't you? Because there is always something going on out there on Elm Street. Just yesterday morning, before Mrs. Gable came over for tea, I was sitting there with my calendar, and her little terrier was out in the front yard making an absolute racket because the recycling truck was coming by. And those trucks are so loud nowadays, with all the clanking and the hydraulic lifts they use... plus, we've had a terrible time with the squirrels getting into the bird feeders this week. I actually had to go down to the hardware store and buy one of those metal baffles, you know, the ones that look like a little upside-down umbrella, just to save the sunflower seeds! 

But you see, even with all that noise and movement right outside the glass, it doesn't pull my attention away from my tasks. I don't look up from my phone list and lose my place because of a squirrel or a loud truck. Honestly, a whole marching band could go down the street, and I'd notice it, of course, but it wouldn't be the cause of my confusion.

Oh, tired. Yes, that’s exactly it. Mentally and physically, just completely drained. It’s a weariness that just sits right in my bones, and it’s been bothering me so much lately. Well, that's just the thing, Doctor, it never really clears up. It's there from the moment I open my eyes until I finally manage to get back to sleep at night. That fogginess... it's exactly what brought me in to see you in the first place, because it's just so relentless.

Anxious or depressed? Well... I suppose I haven't really thought about it in those exact words. It's not so much that I'm sitting around crying or feeling nervous about something specific, like when my husband had his heart surgery years ago—now that was anxiety! I paced the floor of that waiting room until I thought I'd wear a hole in the linoleum, and I couldn't eat a thing for two days. But this... this is different. 

I don't know if I'd call it depressed, exactly. It's more just this terrible frustration and heaviness, like we were just talking about. When you can't remember if you've called Mary about the lemon bars, and you're too exhausted to even stand by the toaster... well, it certainly doesn't make you feel cheerful, does it? It makes me feel quite useless, honestly. I've always been the one people rely on. "Ask Eleanor," they'd say, "Eleanor has the schedule, Eleanor knows the dates." And now Eleanor doesn't even know what day of the week it is half the time! 

So, I don't feel that sharp, panicked sort of anxiety, and I don't feel like crying all the time, but I do feel incredibly weighed down by it all. It's just so disheartening to look at my beautiful calendar and feel like it's written in Greek. But as for being properly depressed or anxious... I'm really not sure if that's the right word for it. It's just the fog and the tiredness taking the joy out of things.

========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
New things? Oh, well... I suppose I haven't really thought about that, because to be perfectly honest, Doctor, I haven't even attempted to learn anything new in quite some time. 

It's funny you mention recipes, because just the other week, my daughter-in-law, Susan—she's a lovely girl, always finding these fascinating, trendy things on the internet—she brought over a recipe for a... oh, what was it... a quinoa and roasted butternut squash salad. She said, "Eleanor, you just have to try making this, it’s so simple and it's wonderful for your heart!" And she left the printout right there on my kitchen island, right next to the fruit bowl. But I just looked at it, and with this awful fog I’ve been telling you about, I thought to myself, "Why on earth would I try to learn what to do with quinoa when I can't even remember if I've called the plumber?" So that piece of paper is still just sitting there, gathering dust. I haven't even tried to read the instructions, let alone actually cook the thing. 

And as for hobbies... well, my goodness, I've been doing my watercolors and my cross-stitch for forty years. I know those brush strokes and stitches like the back of my hand, even if I am mixing up the gallery dates lately. The girls at the senior center actually started a digital photography class last month—they all have those fancy smartphones now, you know, and they want to take proper pictures of their grandbabies and their gardens—and they asked if I wanted to join. Mary even offered to save me a seat near the front. But I just... I couldn't bring myself to even sign up. It just felt like far too much effort to even sit in the chair and try to listen to someone explain buttons and screens. 

So, I really couldn't tell you if I'm having trouble learning new things, because I simply haven't tried. I just haven't had the mind or the energy for it. When you're struggling just to keep your own daily life from falling completely apart, the idea of picking up a new hobby or figuring out a new recipe just seems... well, it seems entirely out of the question. I don't know if I'd fail at it or not, I just haven't tested it out to see.

Now, I have to stare at the calendar, and even when I'm looking right at it, focusing on the numbers is like trying to read underwater. \n\nIt’s just so frustrating because I sit there, trying with all my might to just do the simple task in front of me—like figuring out which volunteer I just called—and my concentration just slips right through my fingers. I end up staring at the paper, feeling completely lost in my own head. So yes, focusing is terribly difficult right now. It’s like my brain just refuses to grip onto the task at hand, no matter how hard I try to force it to pay attention.\n\nDoctor: Do you have trouble finding the right words when you're talking?\n\nPatient: No, no, I wouldn't say that at all. The words are right there. In fact, my daughter always says I have the gift of gab, and I suppose she's right! I've never been one to be at a loss for words. Even when I'm feeling all foggy and mixed up with my scheduling, or when I'm staring at that phone list trying to remember if I just spoke to Linda or if I only thought about calling her... the words themselves come just fine. \n\nLike yesterday, when Mrs. Gable was over for tea. I was telling her all about the new streetlamps—the ones they're putting up on Elm Street, they have that lovely vintage look, sort of like gas lamps, but they're LED, which I suppose is better for the environment, though the light can be a bit harsh if you ask me—anyway, I was explaining all of this to her, and I didn't stumble over a single word. I knew exactly what I wanted to say and how to say it. \n\nIt's really just the organizing of the tasks, the... the mechanics of getting things done in my head that's the problem. The talking part? Oh, that's as easy as breathing. I can chatter away for hours without ever having to stop and search for a word. It's just a shame that all the words in the world don't help me remember if the spring showcase is supposed to be in the main hall or the side gallery! So, no, no trouble with words at all. Just the focus, like we were talking about.\n\nDoctor: Do you find yourself easily distracted by your surroundings?\n\nPatient: Distracted by my surroundings? Oh, heavens no. It really isn't the environment that's the problem. It's not the outside world pulling me away, if that makes sense. \n\nLike I mentioned, I do all my planning and organizing at that little oak table by the window. Now, I suppose you would think sitting by a front window would be terribly distracting, wouldn't you? Because there is always something going on out there on Elm Street. Just yesterday morning, before Mrs. Gable came over for tea, I was sitting there with my calendar, and her little terrier was out in the front yard making an absolute racket because the recycling truck was coming by. And those trucks are so loud nowadays, with all the clanking and the hydraulic lifts they use... plus, we've had a terrible time with the squirrels getting into the bird feeders this week. I actually had to go down to the hardware store and buy one of those metal baffles, you know, the ones that look like a little upside-down umbrella, just to save the sunflower seeds! \n\nBut you see, even with all that noise and movement right outside the glass, it doesn't pull my attention away from my tasks. I don't look up from my phone list and lose my place because of a squirrel or a loud truck. It's that thick soup I was telling you about earlier. The outside world could be as quiet as a church mouse or as loud as a carnival, and I'd still be sitting there staring at my paperwork, completely unable to sort out if Linda is doing the winter showcase or the spring slot. So no, I really wouldn't blame my surroundings at all. The neighborhood is just doing what it always does, it's just my own thoughts that refuse to stay in their proper lanes!\n\nDoctor: Do you feel mentally tired more often than you used to?\n\nPatient: Oh, tired. Yes, that’s exactly it. Mentally and physically, just completely drained. It’s a weariness that just sits right in my bones, and it’s been bothering me so much lately. I mean, I used to have so much energy, you know? I’d be up with the sun, getting the house in order, making sure everything was just so before I even sat down for a cup of coffee. \n\nBut now... well, now I wake up, and even if I’ve been in bed all night, I just feel so heavy. I’ll pull the covers back, and it’s like I haven’t rested at all. But this... this is different. \n\nI don't know if I'd call it depressed, exactly. It's more just this terrible frustration and heaviness, like we were just talking about. When you can't remember if you've called Mary about the lemon bars, and you're too exhausted to even stand by the toaster... well, it certainly doesn't make you feel cheerful, does it? He’s taken over the calendars, checking them every morning and telling me where I need to be. My husband had to take the whole thing over. It’s just so hard, Doctor, going from being the one who manages everything to needing help just to figure out what day it is and who needs calling. It’s like I’m losing my grip on my own life, just one missed appointment and confused schedule at a time.\n\nDoctor: Are you having trouble learning new things, like a new recipe or a new hobby?\n\nPatient: New things? I suppose I haven't really thought about that, because to be perfectly honest, Doctor, I haven't even attempted to learn anything new in quite some time. \n\nIt's funny you mention recipes, because just the other week, my daughter-in-law, Susan—she's a lovely girl, always finding these fascinating, trendy things on the internet—she brought over a recipe for a... oh, what was it... a quinoa and roasted butternut squash salad. Different times of the day... well, let me think about that. You know, I've always been an early riser. For years and years, I'd be up at six, making the coffee, reading the morning paper—my husband used to say I was the only person he knew who could be cheerful before the sun was properly up. It just feels like this... this heavy blanket is over me from the moment I open my eyes until I finally go to sleep. Like yesterday, for instance. I woke up around seven, and usually, that's when my mind would be the sharpest. I'd sit at the kitchen table and plan out the whole day, write down my grocery list, figure out who I needed to call. But yesterday morning, I just sat there staring at the salt and pepper shakers, feeling completely blank. And it didn't get any better by lunchtime. My husband made sandwiches, and I couldn't even remember what kind of mustard we usually buy. 

Then in the afternoon... well, you'd think maybe by three o'clock things would clear up a bit, like how the fog outside burns off when the sun comes out. But no, I was trying to sort through the mail, and it was just as confusing as it had been at breakfast. I couldn't tell the junk mail from the bills. I just stared at a letter from the electric company for what felt like ten minutes, trying to make sense of the numbers. 

And the evenings are no different. After dinner, we usually sit and watch the news, or maybe a program on the television, but my mind is still just... trudging through mud. I can't follow the stories, I can't remember what the newscaster just said five minutes ago. 

So, no, Doctor, I haven't really noticed it being worse in the morning or better in the evening, or anything like that. It's just a constant, unyielding sort of fog. It doesn't seem to care what the clock says. It's just there, all day long, making everything so dreadfully difficult. I keep hoping I'll wake up one morning and it'll be gone, or that maybe after a good cup of tea in the afternoon it'll lift, but it never does. It just stays exactly the same, from morning till night.

I knew exactly what I wanted to say and how to say it. \n\nIt's really just the organizing of the tasks, the... the mechanics of getting things done in my head that's the problem. The talking part? Oh, that's as easy as breathing. I can chatter away for hours without ever having to stop and search for a word. It's just a shame that all the words in the world don't help me remember if the spring showcase is supposed to be in the main hall or the side gallery! So, no, no trouble with words at all. Just the focus, like we were talking about.\n\nDoctor: Do you find yourself easily distracted by your surroundings?\n\nPatient: Distracted by my surroundings? Oh, heavens no. It really isn't the environment that's the problem. It's not the outside world pulling me away, if that makes sense. \n\nLike I mentioned, I do all my planning and organizing at that little oak table by the window. Now, I suppose you would think sitting by a front window would be terribly distracting, wouldn't you? Because there is always something going on out there on Elm Street. Just yesterday morning, before Mrs. Gable came over for tea, I was sitting there with my calendar, and her little terrier was out in the front yard making an absolute racket because the recycling truck was coming by. And those trucks are so loud nowadays, with all the clanking and the hydraulic lifts they use... plus, we've had a terrible time with the squirrels getting into the bird feeders this week. I actually had to go down to the hardware store and buy one of those metal baffles, you know, the ones that look like a little upside-down umbrella, just to save the sunflower seeds! \n\nBut you see, even with all that noise and movement right outside the glass, it doesn't pull my attention away from my tasks. I don't look up from my phone list and lose my place because of a squirrel or a loud truck. Honestly, a whole marching band could go down the street, and I'd notice it, of course, but it wouldn't be the cause of my confusion. \n\nThe confusion is all... well, it's all on the inside. It's that thick soup I was telling you about earlier. The outside world could be as quiet as a church mouse or as loud as a carnival, and I'd still be sitting there staring at my paperwork, completely unable to sort out if Linda is doing the winter showcase or the spring slot. So no, I really wouldn't blame my surroundings at all. The neighborhood is just doing what it always does, it's just my own thoughts that refuse to stay in their proper lanes!\n\nDoctor: Do you feel mentally tired more often than you used to?\n\nPatient: Oh, tired. Yes, that’s exactly it. Mentally and physically, just completely drained. It’s a weariness that just sits right in my bones, and it’s been bothering me so much lately. I mean, I used to have so much energy, you know? ========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
No, actually... no, I don't. And thank heavens for that, because it feels like I need help with absolutely everything else these days! But the medications... no, I manage those just fine on my own. 

You see, I have one of those little plastic pill organizers—you know the ones, with the days of the week printed on the lids in big, bold letters? I bought it years ago at the pharmacy down on Main Street, back when my old doctor first told me I needed to watch my blood pressure. I keep it right on the kitchen counter, exactly two inches from the coffee maker. I've had the exact same routine for... oh, it must be fifteen years now. Every morning, I go into the kitchen to start the coffee—which I still do, even if I just sit there staring at the salt shakers afterward like I told you—and there’s the pillbox, right in front of me. Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday... it’s just muscle memory at this point. I just pop open the little lid and take them with my first sip of water. 

My husband did ask me just the other day, actually... he came into the kitchen and said, "Eleanor, did you remember your morning pills?" And I actually got a little bit snappy with him, I'm ashamed to admit. I told him, "I might not remember what kind of mustard we buy, but I know how to open the Tuesday compartment!" 

So, no, he doesn't need to remind me. It's the one thing—the *only* thing, it feels like sometimes—that I can still do completely on my own without him having to check up on me or write it down on a calendar. It’s just so deeply ingrained in my morning, you know? The coffee, the pills... even if the rest of the day is a complete wash and my mind is full of that awful fog, the pills still get taken without anyone having to say a word.

Well... clearer? No. No, not really. Bathing and dressing? Oh, goodness no, I can still manage all of that on my own. I still get up and wash my face and pick out my clothes, though I will admit it takes me entirely too long just to decide between my navy slacks and my beige ones these days. I just stand there at the closet door. But physical things like that, getting dressed, brushing my teeth... I'm alright with those. 

It’s the other things, Doctor. The things that take... well, organizing and thinking. Like I was telling you before about the calendar, it's just gotten so completely out of hand. I’ve missed doctor visits completely—not just showing up on the wrong day like I did at the dentist, but missing them entirely! It got to the point where my husband, Arthur, bless his heart, he’s had to step in and just take over. He’s helping me with all the phone calls now, and he manages the calendars because I just can't be trusted with them anymore. He even has to make the repair decisions around the house! Just last week, the washing machine started making this dreadful clanking sound during the spin cycle—it's a Maytag, we bought it in 2012 and it's usually very reliable—and I just stood there in the laundry room staring at it, completely overwhelmed, almost in tears because I couldn't figure out who to call or what to say to them. Arthur had to come in, find the manual, call the repairman, and decide whether it was worth fixing the drum or if we needed a new one. 

I used to handle all of that myself, every single bit of it. I ran this house like a top for decades, I handled all the contractors when we redid the roof, I managed all our schedules... and now he has to step in and hold my hand through a simple phone call or a calendar update. So, no, I don't need help putting my shoes on, but... everything else that actually keeps a life running, I just can't seem to do it anymore.

Mary even offered to save me a seat near the front. But I just... I couldn't bring myself to even sign up. It just felt like far too much effort to even sit in the chair and try to listen to someone explain buttons and screens. \n\nSo, I really couldn't tell you if I'm having trouble learning new things, because I simply haven't tried. I just haven't had the mind or the energy for it. When you're struggling just to keep your own daily life from falling completely apart, the idea of picking up a new hobby or figuring out a new recipe just seems... well, it seems entirely out of the question. I don't know if I'd fail at it or not, I just haven't tested it out to see.\n\nDoctor: Do you notice any variation in how foggy your mind feels at different times of the day?\n\nPatient: Different times of the day... well, let me think about that. You know, I've always been an early riser. For years and years, I'd be up at six, making the coffee, reading the morning paper—my husband used to say I was the only person he knew who could be cheerful before the sun was properly up. But now... now, I don't really know if I can say there's a difference. \n\nIt just feels like this... this heavy blanket is over me from the moment I open my eyes until I finally go to sleep. Like yesterday, for instance. I woke up around seven, and usually, that's when my mind would be the sharpest. I'd sit at the kitchen table and plan out the whole day, write down my grocery list, figure out who I needed to call. But yesterday morning, I just sat there staring at the salt and pepper shakers, feeling completely blank. And it didn't get any better by lunchtime. My husband made sandwiches, and I couldn't even remember what kind of mustard we usually buy. \n\nThen in the afternoon... well, you'd think maybe by three o'clock things would clear up a bit, like how the fog outside burns off when the sun comes out. But no, I was trying to sort through the mail, and it was just as confusing as it had been at breakfast. I couldn't tell the junk mail from the bills. I just stared at a letter from the electric company for what felt like ten minutes, trying to make sense of the numbers. \n\nAnd the evenings are no different. After dinner, we usually sit and watch the news, or maybe a program on the television, but my mind is still just... trudging through mud. I can't follow the stories, I can't remember what the newscaster just said five minutes ago. \n\nSo, no, Doctor, I haven't really noticed it being worse in the morning or better in the evening, or anything like that. It's just a constant, unyielding sort of fog. It doesn't seem to care what the clock says. It's just there, all day long, making everything so dreadfully difficult. I keep hoping I'll wake up one morning and it'll be gone, or that maybe after a good cup of tea in the afternoon it'll lift, but it never does. It just stays exactly the same, from morning till night.\n\nDoctor: Do you need help from others to complete your daily routine tasks?\n\nPatient: Oh, yes. I... well, I know I was just rambling on about this very thing a few minutes ago, but yes, I absolutely do need help now. It’s just like I was saying—because I’ve missed those doctor visits so completely, and because I tangled up the senior center schedule so terribly with the bridge club and all of that, my husband has really had to step in and take over. \n\nBless his heart, we've been married for over fifty years, and I have always been the one to run the household. Always. I took pride in it! But now... now he’s the one making all the phone calls, because I just get too confused and can't remember who I'm supposed to be talking to. He’s managing the calendars, sitting down with his reading glasses every single morning to tell me what's what and where we need to be. \n\nAnd the house repairs! I used to handle all of that, like I mentioned with that awful leak under the sink... I would be the one to get the estimates, talk to the workmen, make the decisions, all of it. Now he has to make all those repair decisions, too, because I just look at a problem and my mind goes completely blank. I just can't do my normal routine without him guiding me through it, and it's just so deeply frustrating to need that kind of help when I used to handle every little detail myself without a second thought.\n\nDoctor: Do you need someone to remind you to take your medications?\n\nPatient: No, actually... no, I don't. And thank heavens for that, because it feels like I need help with absolutely everything else these days! But the medications... no, I manage those just fine on my own. \n\nYou see, I have one of those little plastic pill organizers—you know the ones, with the days of the week printed on the lids in big, bold letters? I bought it years ago at the pharmacy down on Main Street, back when my old doctor first told me I needed to watch my blood pressure. I keep it right on the kitchen counter, exactly two inches from the coffee maker. I've had the exact same routine for... oh, it must be fifteen years now. Every morning, I go into the kitchen to start the coffee—which I still do, even if I just sit there staring at the salt shakers afterward like I told you—and there’s the pillbox, right in front of me. Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday... it’s just muscle memory at this point. I just pop open the little lid and take them with my first sip of water. \n\nMy husband did ask me just the other day, actually... he came into the kitchen and said, \"Eleanor, did you remember your morning pills?\" And I actually got a little bit snappy with him, I'm ashamed to admit. I told him, \"I might not remember what kind of mustard we buy, but I know how to open the Tuesday compartment!\" \n\nSo, no, he doesn't need to remind me. It's the one thing—the *only* thing, it feels like sometimes—that I can still do completely on my own without him having to check up on me or write it down on a calendar. It’s just so deeply ingrained in my morning, you know? The coffee, the pills... even if the rest of the day is a complete wash and my mind is full of that awful fog, the pills still get taken without anyone having to say a word.\n\nDoctor: Do you have trouble paying attention to things?\n\nPatient: Well, paying attention... yes, I suppose that's exactly it. That's really the whole reason I'm sitting here talking to you today, to be perfectly honest. I mean, I've been trying to explain this fog, this awful heavy blanket over my thoughts, but it really comes down to the fact that I just can't seem to hold onto anything in my mind long enough to make sense of it. \n\nI keep mixing up the most ridiculously simple things. Things I used to handle with my eyes closed! Like my appointments. I have always been so meticulous about my schedule. I had a little red pocketbook calendar, and everything went in there the minute it was planned. But lately... oh, it's just a disaster. I showed up at the dentist on a Tuesday when my appointment was on a Thursday, and the poor receptionist looked at me like I had two heads. \n\nAnd my volunteer work at the historical society... I've been helping them organize their exhibits for, goodness, it must be nearly a decade. I know that collection backwards and forwards. But last month, I completely jumbled up the dates for the new quilt exhibit. I told the local paper the wrong weekend, and we had people showing up when the quilts were still in storage boxes! It was so embarrassing. I felt my face just burn hot when the director had to explain it to them. \n\nAnd the phone calls... I was supposed to be organizing the phone tree for the church bake sale, which I've done a hundred times. But I found myself sitting at the kitchen table, looking at the list of names, and I couldn't for the life of me remember which volunteer I had already called and which ones I hadn't. I ended up calling poor Mrs. Gable three times in one afternoon to ask if she was baking her famous cherry pie. By the third time, she asked if I was feeling quite alright. \n\nSo, yes, my attention is just... it's like trying to hold water in my hands. It just slips right through. My head is just so foggy, and I can't focus on what's right in front of me, whether it's a date on a calendar or a name on a list. It's just terrifying, Doctor, to lose your grip on the little things that make up your day. I just want to be able to pay attention again like I used to.\n\nDoctor: Do you ever have moments, no matter how brief, where your mind feels clearer than it does right now?\n\nPatient: Well... clearer? No. No, not really. I mean, I sit there sometimes, maybe in the afternoon when the sun is coming through the living room window just right, and I think, \"Oh, maybe this is it, maybe the fog is lifting.\" I'll pick up a magazine, maybe that Better Homes and Gardens subscription I've had since 1982—can you believe I've kept it that long? They used to have the most wonderful articles on rose pruning, back when I had my big garden before we downsized. Anyway, I'll pick it up, thinking my head feels a little lighter, a little less stuffed with cotton. But the moment I actually try to read a paragraph, or the moment the phone rings and I have to actually think about what to say to the person on the other end... it's just right back to that awful, heavy confusion. \n\nIt never really goes away, Doctor. Not even for a minute. It’s like living underwater. I keep waiting to break the surface and take a deep breath of fresh air, where everything is sharp and bright and makes sense again, like it used to just a few months ago. I mean, I used to be sharp as a tack! Everyone said so. \"Ask Eleanor,\" they'd say at the church, \"Eleanor never misses a detail.\" But now? Now it's just one long, continuous stretch of this... this muck in my brain. Morning, noon, and night. Even when I wake up in the middle of the night to use the restroom, I feel it. There are no moments of clarity. None at all. It's just a constant, exhausting struggle to try and peer through the fog, and it just never, ever clears up. Not even for a second.\n\nDoctor: Do you notice any difference in how foggy your mind feels at different times of the day?\n\nPatient: Well, different times of the day... you know, I’ve tried to pay attention to that, I really have. Because my husband, he said to me just last Tuesday—or maybe it was Wednesday, oh, it doesn't matter—he said, \"Eleanor, maybe you're just not a morning person anymore.\" But that’s simply not true! I’ve always been up with the sun. But to answer your question... no. No, there really isn't any difference at all. It doesn't matter if it's six o'clock in the morning or three in the afternoon. \n\nI wake up, and before I even put my slippers on—I have these lovely blue memory foam slippers my daughter got me for Christmas, the ones with the hard soles so you can walk out to get the mail in them without ruining the bottoms—anyway, before I even put them on, that heavy feeling is already there, waiting for me. And then by lunchtime, when I'm trying to figure out if I want half a sandwich or just a bowl of that low-sodium tomato soup... it's just as thick. Arthur just takes care of it, same as he always has. He just writes the checks and tells me when the property taxes are due, and that's that. So, no, I don't need help with it, because I don't really do it in the first place."
